comparison.summary: Five JavaScript approaches are available here. The first uses a shorter exact-ID implementation with comma-separated pair keys and a binary search that returns lo when its bounds meet. It takes expected O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space with bounded-size keys. The rolling-hash and three suffix approaches remain available.
details: The exact-ID version builds power-of-two block levels with flat Maps keyed by `${left},${right}` and assigns each new pair the ID map.size. Each tested window is identified by its first and last block IDs, whose blocks cover the whole sequence. It takes expected O(n log n) time with expected constant-time Map operations and O(n log n) space, treating keys as bounded in size; n is the number of elements. Keys have at most 13 characters under the problem constraints, though creating and hashing those strings still adds overhead.

The rolling-hash version binary-searches the length and groups windows by hash, then compares their actual elements before combining occurrence counts. It takes O(n log n + C) time with expected constant-time Map operations, where C counts all exact element comparisons, and O(n) space. A conservative worst-case time bound is O(n³ log n).
The simple suffix version copies and sorts whole suffixes, then compares neighboring suffixes directly. It is exact, but takes O(n² log n) time with O(n log n) sort comparisons and O(n²) space.

The optimized suffix array version uses rank doubling and stable counting sort, then Kasai’s algorithm for adjacent LCP values. It applies the same unique-prefix formula in O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
The suffix automaton propagates occurrence counts through the shorterId tree and finds the shortest length represented by a node that occurs once. It takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

The older Python solution binary-searches the length and counts rolling hashes without checking the actual elements, taking O(n log n) time and O(n) space. That hash-only comparison is incorrect for nums = [1,20,2,1,20,2]: it returns 3 instead of 2. With base 19, [1,20] and [2,1] both hash to 39, hiding the unique pair [2,1]. All five saved JavaScript solutions return the correct answer 2.

Choosing a base larger than the values prevents that base-19 example from colliding, but modular collisions can still happen. The saved rolling-hash version keeps separate exact-window groups under the same hash; the first solution instead uses exact sequence IDs throughout.

solutions.title: Binary search + exact sequence IDs
solutions.approach: Build exact IDs for blocks whose lengths are powers of two. Single-value blocks use their values as IDs. At each later level, form the comma-separated key `${left},${right}` from the two half IDs; a new key receives map.size as its ID, and an existing key reuses its ID. Then binary-search the smallest valid window length. For each candidate k, choose the largest power-of-two block that fits using Math.floor(Math.log2(k)). Identify each window by its first and last block IDs and count the comma-separated keys. These two blocks cover the whole window, so matching keys mean equal sequences. If a key appears once, keep mid as the upper bound; otherwise move the lower bound to mid + 1. Return lo when the bounds meet.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) expected, treating short keys as bounded in size and assuming expected constant-time Map operations
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n log n) for bounded-size keys
notes: The comma-separated string preserves both integer IDs and their order. IDs are local to one block level; 0 is valid, so use map.has(key) to check whether a pair already has an ID.
The first and last blocks cover the whole window and may overlap. When k is a power of two, both IDs describe the same block, and the window is still counted once.
Keys have at most 13 characters under the problem constraints. Creating and hashing strings adds overhead, while their bounded size gives the stated expected O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space.

#### 1. Input and the result we want

Use `nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]`. Set `n = nums.length = 5`. We want the shortest continuous subarray that occurs **exactly once**. Occurrences at different starting indices count separately, even when they overlap.

| Index | Value |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 |
| 4 | 1 |

The code first builds exact IDs for blocks of lengths `1`, `2`, and `4`. It then binary-searches a candidate length. Each window is identified by its first-block ID and last-block ID, joined with a comma. Counting those string keys counts identical windows exactly.

#### 2. Start with one-value blocks

Initialize `levels = [nums]`. Level `0` describes blocks of length `1`: the value itself is its ID. Value `1` has ID `1`; value `2` has ID `2`. This assignment stores the existing `nums` array as the first level; it does not scan or copy the values.

```text
level 0, length 1: [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]
```

At each later level, split a block into equal left and right halves. Their IDs form a string key with a comma: `left = 1` and `right = 2` produce `"1,2"`. A new key gets the ID `map.size`; an existing key reuses its ID.

In preprocessing snapshots, `"1,2" → 0` means that the pair of half IDs `(1, 2)` has been assigned whole-block ID `0`. The ID labels are local to their level; each new level starts with an empty Map. ID `0` at one level can describe a different sequence from ID `0` at another level.

#### 3. Build level 1: blocks of length 2

Initialize the outer loop with `len = 2`.

Check `len <= n`: `2 <= 5` is true. Calculate `half = len / 2 = 2 / 2 = 1`.

`levels.length = 1`, so read `prev = levels[1 - 1] = levels[0] = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]`. These IDs describe blocks of length `1`.

Create `ids = []` and a new empty `map`. Its `map.size` is `0`. Initialize the inner loop with `i = 0`.

```text
(empty Map)
```

**Block at `i = 0`: `[1, 2]`.** Check `i + len <= n`: `0 + 2 <= 5`, or `2 <= 5`, is true.

1. Read `left = prev[0] = 1`. The left half covers indices `0` through `0` and contains `[1]`.

2. Read `right = prev[0 + 1] = prev[1] = 2`. The right half covers indices `1` through `1` and contains `[2]`.

3. Build `key` by joining `left = 1`, the comma, and `right = 2`: `key = "1,2"`.

Before the lookup, `ids = []` and `map.size = 0`. The pair Map is:

```text
(empty Map)
```

Check `map.has("1,2")`: it is `false`, so `!map.has("1,2")` is `true`.

The key is new. Read `map.size = 0` **before** adding it, then execute `map.set("1,2", 0)`. This block gets ID `0`. The Map now has `1` entry, so `map.size` becomes `1`.

Read `map.get("1,2") = 0` and execute `ids.push(0)`. Now `ids = [0]`. The pair Map after this block is:

```text
"1,2" → 0
```

Increase `i` from `0` to `1`.

**Block at `i = 1`: `[2, 1]`.** Check `i + len <= n`: `1 + 2 <= 5`, or `3 <= 5`, is true.

1. Read `left = prev[1] = 2`. The left half covers indices `1` through `1` and contains `[2]`.

2. Read `right = prev[1 + 1] = prev[2] = 1`. The right half covers indices `2` through `2` and contains `[1]`.

3. Build `key` by joining `left = 2`, the comma, and `right = 1`: `key = "2,1"`.

Before the lookup, `ids = [0]` and `map.size = 1`. The pair Map is:

```text
"1,2" → 0
```

Check `map.has("2,1")`: it is `false`, so `!map.has("2,1")` is `true`.

The key is new. Read `map.size = 1` **before** adding it, then execute `map.set("2,1", 1)`. This block gets ID `1`. The Map now has `2` entries, so `map.size` becomes `2`.

Read `map.get("2,1") = 1` and execute `ids.push(1)`. Now `ids = [0, 1]`. The pair Map after this block is:

```text
"1,2" → 0
"2,1" → 1
```

Increase `i` from `1` to `2`.

**Block at `i = 2`: `[1, 2]`.** Check `i + len <= n`: `2 + 2 <= 5`, or `4 <= 5`, is true.

1. Read `left = prev[2] = 1`. The left half covers indices `2` through `2` and contains `[1]`.

2. Read `right = prev[2 + 1] = prev[3] = 2`. The right half covers indices `3` through `3` and contains `[2]`.

3. Build `key` by joining `left = 1`, the comma, and `right = 2`: `key = "1,2"`.

Before the lookup, `ids = [0, 1]` and `map.size = 2`. The pair Map is:

```text
"1,2" → 0
"2,1" → 1
```

Check `map.has("1,2")`: it is `true`, so `!map.has("1,2")` is `false`.

The key already exists with ID `0`. Skip `map.set`; keep that ID. `map.size` stays `2`.

Read `map.get("1,2") = 0` and execute `ids.push(0)`. Now `ids = [0, 1, 0]`. The pair Map after this block is:

```text

"2,1" → 1
```

Increase `i` from `2` to `3`.

**Block at `i = 3`: `[2, 1]`.** Check `i + len <= n`: `3 + 2 <= 5`, or `5 <= 5`, is true.

1. Read `left = prev[3] = 2`. The left half covers indices `3` through `3` and contains `[2]`.

2. Read `right = prev[3 + 1] = prev[4] = 1`. The right half covers indices `4` through `4` and contains `[1]`.

3. Build `key` by joining `left = 2`, the comma, and `right = 1`: `key = "2,1"`.

Before the lookup, `ids = [0, 1, 0]` and `map.size = 2`. The pair Map is:

```text
"1,2" → 0
"2,1" → 1
```

Check `map.has("2,1")`: it is `true`, so `!map.has("2,1")` is `false`.

The key already exists with ID `1`. Skip `map.set`; keep that ID. `map.size` stays `2`.

Read `map.get("2,1") = 1` and execute `ids.push(1)`. Now `ids = [0, 1, 0, 1]`. The pair Map after this block is:

```text
"1,2" → 0
"2,1" → 1
```

Increase `i` from `3` to `4`.

At `i = 4`, check `4 + 2 <= 5`, or `6 <= 5`: false. The inner loop ends.

Execute `levels.push(ids)`, saving `[0, 1, 0, 1]` as level `1`:

```text
level 0, length 1: [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]
level 1, length 2: [0, 1, 0, 1]
```

Execute `len *= 2`: `2 × 2 = 4`.

`levels.length = 2`, so read `prev = levels[2 - 1] = levels[1] = [0, 1, 0, 1]`. These IDs describe blocks of length `2`.

Create `ids = []` and a new empty `map`. Its `map.size` is `0`. Initialize the inner loop with `i = 0`.

```text
(empty Map)
```

**Block at `i = 0`: `[1, 2, 1, 2]`.** Check `i + len <= n`: `0 + 4 <= 5`, or `4 <= 5`, is true.

1. Read `left = prev[0] = 0`. The left half covers indices `0` through `1` and contains `[1, 2]`.

2. Read `right = prev[0 + 2] = prev[2] = 0`. The right half covers indices `2` through `3` and contains `[1, 2]`.

3. Build `key` by joining `left = 0`, the comma, and `right = 0`: `key = "0,0"`.

Before the lookup, `ids = []` and `map.size = 0`. The pair Map is:

```text
(empty Map)
```

Check `map.has("0,0")`: it is `false`, so `!map.has("0,0")` is `true`.

The key is new. Read `map.size = 0` **before** adding it, then execute `map.set("0,0", 0)`. This block gets ID `0`. The Map now has `1` entry, so `map.size` becomes `1`.

Read `map.get("0,0") = 0` and execute `ids.push(0)`. Now `ids = [0]`. The pair Map after this block is:

```text
"0,0" → 0
```

Increase `i` from `0` to `1`.

**Block at `i = 1`: `[2, 1, 2, 1]`.** Check `i + len <= n`: `1 + 4 <= 5`, or `5 <= 5`, is true.

1. Read `left = prev[1] = 1`. The left half covers indices `1` through `2` and contains `[2, 1]`.

2. Read `right = prev[1 + 2] = prev[3] = 1`. The right half covers indices `3` through `4` and contains `[2, 1]`.

3. Build `key` by joining `left = 1`, the comma, and `right = 1`: `key = "1,1"`.

Before the lookup, `ids = [0]` and `map.size = 1`. The pair Map is:

```text
"0,0" → 0
```

Check `map.has("1,1")`: it is `false`, so `!map.has("1,1")` is `true`.

The key is new. Read `map.size = 1` **before** adding it, then execute `map.set("1,1", 1)`. This block gets ID `1`. The Map now has `2` entries, so `map.size` becomes `2`.

Read `map.get("1,1") = 1` and execute `ids.push(1)`. Now `ids = [0, 1]`. The pair Map after this block is:

```text
"0,0" → 0
"1,1" → 1
```

Increase `i` from `1` to `2`.

At `i = 2`, check `2 + 4 <= 5`, or `6 <= 5`: false. The inner loop ends.

Execute `levels.push(ids)`, saving `[0, 1]` as level `2`:

```text
level 0, length 1: [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]
level 1, length 2: [0, 1, 0, 1]
level 2, length 4: [0, 1]
```

Execute `len *= 2`: `4 × 2 = 8`.

Check the next outer-loop condition: `8 <= 5` is false. Precomputation ends. No level for length `8` is built. Level `2`, for length `4`, is precomputed even though neither search check in this example selects it: preprocessing builds every power-of-two length that fits inside `n`.

**Why `.has()` matters for ID `0`.** At level `1`, the key `"1,2"` received ID `0`. At `i = 2`, `map.has("1,2")` was `true`, so that ID was correctly reused. Testing `!map.get("1,2")` instead would wrongly treat its value `0` as missing, because `0` is falsy.

#### 5. Why the IDs and pair keys are exact

**Exact IDs, level by level.** At level `0`, equal IDs mean equal individual values. At the next level, a block is determined by its left half and right half. If both half IDs match, both half sequences match, so the whole blocks match. Each different pair key receives a different ID: `map.size` counts how many distinct keys already exist, and each insertion increases that size by one. No entries are deleted. This reasoning applies at every new level.

**The comma preserves both integer IDs and their order.** The key `"1,23"` differs from `"12,3"`; the separator prevents the ambiguity that joining digits without a comma would create. `"1,2"` also differs from `"2,1"`. The IDs are integers, whose decimal text contains no comma, so one key corresponds to one ordered pair. A JavaScript Map compares complete string keys for equality; any hashing inside the Map does not merge different strings.

**Two blocks cover a complete window.** In `hasUnique(k)`, `k` is the candidate window length. The code calculates `level = Math.floor(Math.log2(k))` and `len = 2 ** level`. `Math.log2(k)` asks which power of two gives `k`; flooring its result chooses the largest power-of-two length that fits. Therefore `len <= k < 2 × len`.

The first block covers indices `i` through `i + len - 1`. The last block begins at `i + k - len` and ends at `i + k - 1`. Together they cover the whole window, overlapping by `2 × len - k` elements. No middle positions are left out.

For `k = 3`, `len = 2`. In `[1, 2, 1]` at start `0`, the first block `[1, 2]` covers indices `0, 1`, and the last block `[2, 1]` covers indices `1, 2`. They overlap at index `1`. If the first and last exact IDs both match another window, every position of the two windows matches.

When `k = len`, the first and last blocks are the same complete window. The key repeats its ID, such as `"0,0"`, but the loop still records that window only once.

#### 6. Initialize the search and keep the shortest length in range

A unique window shorter than `n` can be extended right if there is a following element. If it reaches the right edge, being shorter than `n` guarantees an element to its left, so extend it left. If the extended window occurred twice, the original window would occur twice at the same offset within it, which is impossible. Therefore, after one length succeeds, every larger length succeeds.

Set `lo = 1` and `hi = n = 5`. The shortest valid length stays inside `[lo, hi]`. The upper bound is valid initially because the whole array occurs once. There is no separate `answer` variable.

If a midpoint works, set `hi = mid`: it could still be the shortest valid length, so keep it in the range. If it fails, all lengths up to that midpoint fail, so set `lo = mid + 1`. When the two bounds meet, that one remaining length is the result.

solutions.approach: Binary-search the smallest length for which some continuous subarray occurs exactly once. For each tested length, build the first window’s polynomial hash, then slide by removing the outgoing value’s weighted contribution, shifting the remaining weights, and adding the incoming value. Store a list of representative windows and occurrence counts under each hash. When hashes match, compare the actual elements before increasing a count; different sequences keep separate groups. After recording every window, a group with count 1 means this length works, so search shorter lengths. Otherwise, search longer lengths. A unique window can always be extended while remaining unique, which makes binary search valid.

#### 8. A collision example: one length-2 check

This is a separate, focused illustration of hash collisions at **fixed length 2**, not a second binary-search trace. Use `nums = [1, 9994, 100000, 10001, 1, 9994, 100000, 10001]`. Its maximum value is `100000`, so `BASE = 100000 + 1 = 100001`; `MOD` remains `1000000007`.

For two values, the polynomial is `first × BASE + second`:

- `[1, 9994]`: `1 × 100001 + 9994 = 109995`; `109995 % 1000000007 = 109995`.

- `[10001, 1]`: `10001 × 100001 + 1 = 1000110002`; `1000110002 % 1000000007 = 109995`.

The raw values differ by exactly `1000110002 - 109995 = 1000000007`, so the remainder is the same even though the arrays are different.

All seven length-2 windows have these hashes:

| Start | Window | Hash |
|---:|---|---:|
| `0` | `[1, 9994]` | `109995` |
| `1` | `[9994, 100000]` | `999509994` |
| `2` | `[100000, 10001]` | `109931` |
| `3` | `[10001, 1]` | `109995` |
| `4` | `[1, 9994]` | `109995` |
| `5` | `[9994, 100000]` | `999509994` |
| `6` | `[100000, 10001]` | `109931` |

Follow the bucket for hash `109995`:

1. At start `0`, no bucket exists. Create an empty list and push `{ start: 0, count: 1 }` for `[1, 9994]`. The bucket becomes `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }]`.

2. Starts `1` and `2` use other hash buckets, so this bucket stays `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }]`.

3. At start `3`, the hash is also `109995`. Before recording, the bucket is `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }]`. Visit its group and call `sameWindow(0, 3)`. At `offset = 0`, `0 < 2` is true. Compare `nums[0 + 0] = 1` with `nums[3 + 0] = 10001`. They differ, so return `false` immediately; offset `1` is not visited. The existing group’s count stays `1`. No more groups exist, so push `{ start: 3, count: 1 }`. The bucket becomes `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`.

4. At start `4`, the hash is `109995` again. Before recording, the bucket is `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`. Visit the first group and call `sameWindow(0, 4)`. At offset `0`, `0 < 2` is true and `nums[0] = 1` equals `nums[4] = 1`; advance to offset `1`. At offset `1`, `1 < 2` is true and `nums[1] = 9994` equals `nums[5] = 9994`; advance to offset `2`. Now `2 < 2` is false, so return `true`. Increase the first group’s count `1 → 2` and return from `recordWindow`; the second group is not compared. The bucket becomes `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`.

5. Starts `5` and `6` use other hash buckets. The final collision bucket remains `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`. The other two buckets each contain one group with count `2`.

6. The final count scan visits hash `109995` first. Its start-`0` group has count `2`, so it continues. Its start-`3` group has count `1`, so `hasUnique(2)` returns `true` immediately; the other buckets are not visited. `[10001, 1]` is unique.

Every individual value in this example occurs twice, so length `1` fails and the correct shortest length is `2`. Counting only hashes would merge the two different groups into one count of `3`, miss this unique pair, and incorrectly return `3` for the problem. Comparing the actual elements keeps the answer exact.

#### 9. Time, space, and what the extra comparisons cost

Let `n` be the number of elements and `C` be the total number of element comparisons performed by `sameWindow` across **all tested lengths**. `C` includes comparisons between truly identical windows as well as comparisons caused by accidental hash collisions. The main example performs `3 + 3 + 4 = 10` such comparisons.

The maximum scan costs `O(n)`. Hash construction, sliding, and creating or updating at most one group per window cost `O(n)` per check, assuming expected constant-time Map operations. Every candidate group visited during the bucket search performs at least one element comparison, so that search overhead is covered by `C`. Binary search tests `O(log n)` lengths, so total time is **`O(n log n + C)`**. A conservative worst-case bound is **`O(n³ log n)`**: a check can compare `O(n²)` pairs of windows and inspect up to `O(n)` elements per pair.

Space is **`O(n)`**: one check stores at most one group per window, using a start index and a count. It does not copy subarrays. The next check creates a fresh Map, and the old one is no longer needed.

Exact comparisons can be expensive on large inputs with many repeated windows. The optimized suffix array and suffix automaton solutions below avoid this repeated element-by-element verification.

solutions.title: Simple suffix sorting + LCP
solutions.approach: Copy every suffix and sort those arrays lexicographically. For each suffix, compare its elements with the previous and next suffix to find their longest common prefixes (LCP). A unique prefix needs max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 elements; take the smallest such length that fits inside its suffix.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n² log n) with O(n log n) sort comparisons
notes: This version makes the steps easier to follow, but copies n(n + 1) / 2 elements. Use an optimized version for large inputs such as 100,000 numbers.

solutions.title: Optimized suffix array + LCP
solutions.approach: Sort suffix starting indices without copying the suffixes: rank doubling compares increasingly long prefixes using stable counting sorts. Kasai’s algorithm calculates neighboring LCP values while reusing matches from the previous suffix. For each suffix, compute max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 and take the smallest length that fits inside that suffix.
notes: This optimized version uses the separate function name smallestUniqueSubarraySuffixArray.

solutions.title: Suffix automaton
solutions.approach: Build a suffix automaton that groups subarrays sharing the same ending positions. Add each node’s occurrence count to its shorterId parent after processing its children. For a node seen exactly once, nodes[shorterId].maxLength + 1 is its shortest unique length; take the minimum of those lengths.
notes: Preserved naming: currNum, newId, lastId, shorterId, nextId, cloneId, ROOT_ID, and NO_ID. Transitions remain plain JavaScript objects.
